title: Why £100 million of CCP capital can absorb different expected losses
summary: The Bank of England’s analysis of a clearing house’s second contribution of its own capital to the default waterfall asks how much economic exposure a stated amount actually creates. Placed behind surviving members’ prefunded default fund, that capital starts absorbing losses only after the fund is exhausted. Placed alongside it, the same capital participates in a wider range of losses. Under the central illustration, £100 million in the later position has the same expected loss to the clearing house as approximately £32 million in the earlier position. The comparison equates one specified outcome for the clearing house. It does not establish that the two designs have equivalent resources available in a severe default.

Table A holds the first layers constant. The defaulting member’s variation margin, initial margin and default fund contribution are used first, followed by the clearing house’s first contribution. Under the single-tranche design, the non-defaulters’ prefunded contributions are then exhausted before the clearing house’s second contribution is reached. Under the pro-rata design, members’ prefunded resources and the second contribution share losses at that point. In either case, sufficiently large losses reach unfunded resources. The ranking therefore changes the probability of a call on the clearing house even when neither the defaulter’s resources nor the face amount of that second contribution changes.

Section 4 assigns a 99.9% probability to outcomes in which the later tranche is untouched. In the remaining illustrative outcomes, it is partly consumed with 0.01% probability and fully consumed with 0.09% probability. The calculation assumes that losses falling inside the tranche use half of it on average. Multiplying each possible loss by its probability gives an expected £95,000 loss on £100 million of second capital. These are scenario probabilities, without an empirically estimated frequency for a named clearing house.

Moving the tranche forward changes the arithmetic. In the central pro-rata case the probability of avoiding any call falls to 99.5%. The paper holds the full-loss event at 0.09%, leaving 0.41% for partial consumption. With the same assumption about average loss inside the layer, expected loss on £100 million rises to £295,000. Reducing the nominal pro-rata tranche to roughly 32% of its previous size restores the £95,000 benchmark. Section 6 illustrates what the units mean. If the single tranche were 25% of regulatory capital, the central equivalent would be about 8% of regulatory capital, rather than 32% of regulatory capital.

The sensitivity range is wide. Changing the no-call probability for the pro-rata tranche to 99% or 99.7% produces equivalent nominal amounts of roughly 17% or 49% of the single tranche respectively. The Bank cautions against reading those no-call probabilities as initial margin confidence levels. Several resources can absorb losses before the second capital is reached. The exercise also holds tail frequencies fixed as tranche sizes change, and assumes uniform losses within each layer. Actual concentrations, collateral values and the distribution of losses near the attachment point could change the relationship. The paper therefore offers a way to compare the incentives and exposure associated with waterfall design, to be used alongside CCP-specific stress losses and member positions.

questions.question: Where do the actual stress losses sit relative to the point at which CCP capital joins the default fund?
questions.detail: The note demonstrates how much the equivalent tranche changes when the frequency of first loss moves. It supplies illustrative probabilities rather than member-level loss observations. For a clearing member assessing mutualised risk, examine the CCP’s stressed portfolios, collateral assumptions and default fund contributions. Reconstruct the loss distribution around each attachment point, including concentrated defaults, before transferring the 32% comparison to that service.

questions.question: How would reducing the combined prefunded resources change recourse to unfunded member payments?
questions.detail: Section 5 holds the full-loss probability fixed so that it can isolate the effect of moving the tranche. That choice leaves open whether a smaller total prefunded cushion would increase the size or frequency of subsequent cash assessments. Those assessments matter for a member’s stress liquidity budget. Consult the service’s rulebook and scenario-level recovery analysis, rerunning each candidate structure on the same losses and tracing what remains for members to pay.

questions.question: Does partial consumption typically fall near half of the layer?
questions.detail: The calculation assumes it does, but a distribution concentrated just inside the attachment point would produce different average losses from one clustered near exhaustion. A clearing member comparing the incentives borne by CCP shareholders needs the conditional loss amounts as well as the probability of being hit. Request simulated default-management losses before and after successive resources are used, then compare the conditional severity under the two rankings.

limitation: All probabilities and amounts are illustrative. The note does not estimate a loss frequency, an optimal tranche size or the relative safety of two actual clearing services.
